idiom_name: container entity + component slots + explicit update dispatch
implementation_notes:
Language-neutral form: make each domain of behaviour a small object with one narrow contract (typically a single update/render/handle-event hook) that knows nothing about the container; make the object itself a container holding the attached components plus the state shared across domains (identity, position, health) and forwarding requests to them. Compose each entity kind once, in an assembler or prefab, never at scattered call sites. Dispatch is either per entity (the container forwards every request to its components in order) or per component type (a system owns all components of one class and runs them as a group, which is what you need when update order must be deterministic); the data-oriented variant replaces the container's per-entity slot list with per-component-type storage (arrays of struct or struct of arrays) and queries that walk archetypes or sparse sets. The key distinction is that components carry no behaviour of their own in the pure form.

Three dominant storage strategies exist. (1) Archetype/table-based (Flecs, Unity DOTS, Bevy, Unreal Mass): entities with the same component set share a table; components are stored column-wise in contiguous arrays, giving excellent iteration cache locality and fast archetype-based queries. (2) Sparse-set based (EnTT, Shipyard): each component type is its own sparse set indexed by entity id; fast O(1) add/remove but less cache-friendly for bulk iteration. (3) Bitset-based (Specs, EntityX): a bitset marks which entities have which components; simple but scales poorly with component count. Reactive ECS (Entitas) uses signals from mutations to drive which entities match queries.
code_sketch:
entity = container(input=PlayerInput(), physics=Physics(), graphics=Graphics())
loop(dt):
    for c in entity.components:
        c.update(entity, dt)        # or: systems run in a defined order
# container: identity + pan-domain state
# components: one capability each + their own state
pitfalls: Sharing everything through the container: every component reads and writes the same fields, so the coupling removed from the class diagram moves into the container's data.
Leaving dispatch order implicit - 'update the components in the order they were attached' is a contract nobody wrote down; make the order explicit (systems) as soon as correctness depends on it.
Letting components reference sibling components directly, recreating the dependency web the split was meant to remove.
Attaching or detaching components in the middle of a dispatch pass, so some parts see the old set and some the new one.
Mixing encapsulated behaviour into components (calling c.update() directly on a component) converts the pattern back to an EC framework and loses the data-oriented iteration benefits.
Frequent structural changes (add/remove component) during gameplay cause archetype fragmentation in table-based ECS, scattering entities across many small tables and hurting cache performance.
Using a component as a 'communication bus' by writing and reading arbitrary fields from it creates hidden coupling between systems that is hard to reason about and debug.

Wrong move: assume archetype storage is automatically the fastest -> failure: entities whose component set changes at runtime fragment across many small archetype tables and real workloads regress badly (Moonside Games reports a storage rework taking Samurai Gunn 2 from ~300-500 FPS to ~5 FPS) -> instead: choose sparse-set/ergonomic storage when composition is dynamic, and profile before committing to archetypes.

Wrong move: treat 'ECS gives data locality' as guaranteed -> failure: real systems read several component types per entity, so each type crossed is another cache miss plus an indirection lookup, and the ECS build ends up slower than plain arrays -> instead: co-locate the fields one hot system iterates into a single component, split hot from cold data, and verify with a profiler.

Wrong move: adopt ECS as a wholesale replacement for ordinary classes -> failure: event-driven, deeply hierarchical or state-machine-heavy logic gets harder to express and developer velocity drops with no measured performance gain -> instead: apply the pattern where bulk data-driven processing and runtime composition are the actual requirements and keep concrete classes elsewhere.
